title: [Master Express Lesson 7] Master this lesson, and you'll fully handle CLO texture processing!
description: After last week's special effects live broadcast ended, we received quite a few awesome special effects masterpieces~ After learning this texture processing, can any friends also submit a piece or hand in a little assignment to Xiao C? QAQ, Xiao C's rainbow praise is ready to go~~ Submissions to: tougao@clo3d.com~~
transcript:
Hello everyone, welcome to this live broadcast, I am your host Lidia.  
This live broadcast will cover content about the processing of building materials.  
As you all know, the real performance of building materials is divided into two parts.  
The first is the physical properties of building materials, which affect the physical effects of building materials, including the elasticity of the fabric, etc.  
This is virtual data and virtual fabric obtained after fabric measurement and fabrication.  
We won’t discuss this part today. If you want to know more about this part, you can visit the link in our introduction.  
The second part is the physical properties of building materials.  
The physical properties of building materials do not affect the physical effects of building materials but rather the texture of the building materials.  
These physical properties include rigidity, three-dimensionality, glossiness, etc.  
In other words, when we have a real piece of fabric in our hands, what steps should we take to make this piece of fabric appear more realistic in our 3D clothing?  
Today’s live broadcast is a theory topic.  
As we know, fabric processing involves three basic steps.  
The first step is ironing.  
We need to iron our fabric first.  
This step is very important for the next step of plant scanning.  
Next is scanning.  
Why scanning and not taking pictures? There are two very important reasons for this.  
First, the scanned image and the size of the fabric are 1:1.  
Second, scanning images can basically ensure that the light received by the fabric is even.  
This is impossible to achieve by photography.  
So scanning is more convenient.  
After that, we can use bi-consequence processing.  
The third step is the processing of our scanned image.  
Now let’s talk about what we need to scan.  
First is our scanning device.  
We can use a connected scanning device directly in our office.  
Can you hear me clearly? Let me bring the microphone closer.  
Hello, can you hear me clearly? Okay, let’s talk about our scanning device first.  
We can use our integrated scanning device.  
Additionally, there are professional physical scanning devices like VZoom.  
This scanning device is compatible with software.  
It is very convenient to scan images and calculate them through software to generate a 3D sticker.  
In today’s live broadcast, we will teach you how to generate a 3D sticker in another way.  
As for what a 3D sticker is, I will explain later.  
Other scanning devices include tablet-type and portable scanners.  
The second point is the scanning settings.  
We need to set the resolution of our scanning device to 300 dpi or above.  
The sound is a little unstable. Let me adjust it.  
Hello, can you hear me better now? Okay, let’s continue.  
The third point is to ensure the fabric is positioned correctly before scanning.  
After scanning, we process the pattern.  
Pattern processing involves four aspects.  
First, if there is a color difference when scanning, we need to adjust the color in Photoshop to a more realistic color.  
Second, repetition of the pattern — how to process the scanned pattern into a quadrilateral. I will explain shortly.  
Third, 1:1 ratio — ensure the DPI of the scanned pattern and the DPI of the processed pattern later are the same.  
Fourth, introduction to the concept of plant pattern.  
We can see our pattern on this dress.  
The one on the left is a correct quadrilateral.  
The one on the right lacks the quadrilateral effect and is a completely incorrect pattern.  
It is very important to process it into a correct quadrilateral.  
Regarding the 1:1 effect, the pattern on the left matches the scanned pattern, while the one on the right has a modified pixel value, making the pattern larger.  
We must maintain consistent pixel values for the pattern.  
Next is the introduction to the concept of our plant pattern.  
We need several pictures: a plant file from Yang-Gaorong in our system fabric warehouse.  
The picture on the far left is a fabric pattern most people are familiar with, obtained through scanning.  
The two pictures in the middle are our hair line and…  
The picture on the far right is a plant pattern.  
It is a plant made of hair.  
So we obtain the base fabric from the plant.  
Then we add a plant to the base fabric.  
The plant textures correspond to our fabric properties so that when the plant is purchased next, it matches the desired fabric.  
You can use this plant to buy raw material from the fabric warehouse, following the texture rules of the lab.  
Okay, let me show you.  
First, approach each plant in your fabric.  
Then the second element is what is called the plant.  
We are about to start the request for a plant on that fabric.  
You can see that this is a plant called Bedmium or one you can observe.  
This plant runs into our fabric first and plays its role in compliance and relaxation through the sense of shadow to reflect the roughness of our object.  
At the bottom of the texture in our attribute editor is the position of our hair line sticker, which is the effect of this blue-purple picture.  
Below is a strength parameter.  
Let’s look at the strength range.  
In our system, it can be set from -50 to +50.  
When the strength is 0, there is no roughness at all.  
When the strength is 50, roughness is strongest.  
You can see a change at the middle value 25.  
A negative value reverses the roughness effect.  
Next is our hallucination picture.  
The hallucination picture is used to display a 3D sticker with a real feeling of roughness in the texture.  
Look at our two dresses: the one on the left has no hallucination picture; the one on the right does.  
The left looks completely flat like paper.  
Zoom in, the right has a three-dimensional effect, created through the hallucination picture.  
That is, below our hair sticker, there is a hallucination picture.  
We display this through the hallucination picture.  
This is a black and white or gray picture.  
There are several fingers below it.  
We can set these fingers to achieve different hallucination effects.  
You can see the hallucination picture — it’s a gray picture, on the left above us.  
The right one has a high silk blur in Photoshop applied, giving a smoother effect.  
Below is the hallucination degree — the level of hallucination.  
The level of hallucination measures the thickness of the most prominent position.  
When the level is 1, the white area is the highest hallucination, black has none.  
Zero level means no thickness.  
At level 1 millimeter, the white claw protrudes 1 mm.  
At level 2, it is obviously higher.  
Next is movement.  
Movement means the hallucination picture can move a certain distance.  
This is set because some fabrics are thick, like wool.  
We may add hallucination to areas where the fabric texture floats slightly by adding a positive value.  
You can see the texture moving slightly.  
Next is cutting height.  
Cutting height corresponds to the height on the sticker.  
If set to 0.5, we cut the geometric shape of areas lower than 0.5.  
You can see the effect.  
Next is particle structure.  
The hallucination picture principle adds a horizontal grid to build a three-dimensional grid for the protruding effect.  
This effect must be viewed in the convection window of our 3D software; it cannot be seen in the actual 3D window without the convection engine enabled.  
Particle structure controls grid size.  
If too large, the grid looks rough and the image lacks delicacy.  
Reducing particle structure to 1 makes it more delicate.  
The hallucination picture consumes a lot of memory to render, so for large areas, particle structure should not be lower than 1.  
Finally, continuity.  
After applying the hallucination picture to the object, continuity makes the gaps continuous.  
Next, highlight picture.  
The highlight picture defines the surface brightness of the object as a 3D sticker.  
For example, I added a highlight picture to this cheongsam on the right side.  
In the highlight picture, black areas are brightest; white parts are unlit.  
The black floral pattern on the skirt now has a high level of light effect.  
Next is strength, which corresponds to reflection intensity.  
The roughness value below determines the surface roughness.  
The larger the value, the rougher the surface.  
When roughness is 50, the fabric looks more luminous.  
Reflection intensity below refers to the amount of light reflected on the fabric; the larger the value, the stronger the reflection.  
At 70, reflection effect is strongest.  
Now that we have discussed the thought process and concept of 3D stickers, let’s move on to today’s topic.  
Before starting, I will talk about different types of plant processing.  
First, fabric color.  
Today we introduce software called PixPlant.  
In this software, we do continuous processing of fabric color and produce a 3D sticker.  
Second is the plant of hard flower fabric.  
There are three types of hard flower plants.  
First, you already have a hard flower fabric.  
Second, you have a plant; then we scan it directly and process it continuously to generate the 3D sticker; this requires cooperation with PixPlant.  
Third, if only a flower is in hand and you want to express fabric texture with this flower, you can do compounding in Photoshop combining flower and technique.  
Third type is hollow plant, e.g., laser net sand.  
How to make it hollow?  
Use scanning technique and Photoshop to draw the pattern.  
Last is compounding material plant.  
Layer processing is needed in Photoshop.  
This is what we introduce today.  
Next, we introduce plastic fabric.

chunks.content: # Master Express Lesson 7: CLO Texture Processing This document covers detailed procedures and technical concepts for processing fabric textures in CLO, focusing on physical texture properties, scanning techniques, pattern processing, 3D sticker creation, and software tools like PixPlant and Photoshop. --- ## Overview of Fabric Physical and Virtual Properties This section explains the distinction between virtual fabric data and physical fabric properties essential for realistic 3D clothing texture rendering. - **Virtual Fabric Data:** Includes elasticity and other physical effects obtained through fabric measurement and simulation; not covered here. - **Physical Fabric Properties:** Affect texture realism in 3D models, including rigidity, three-dimensionality, glossiness, and surface roughness. - Key question: How to transform a real fabric sample into a realistic 3D representation in CLO. --- ## Three Basic Steps of Fabric Texture Processing This section outlines the essential workflow for fabric texture processing: ironing, scanning, and bi-consequence processing. 1. **Ironing:** Prepare the fabric by ironing to ensure smoothness and consistency; critical for quality scanning. 2. **Scanning:** - Use scanners instead of photography for: - 1:1 scale accuracy between scanned image and fabric. - Even lighting, which photography cannot guarantee. - Scanning devices include: - Integrated office scanners. - Professional scanners like VZoom compatible with 3D software. - Tablet-type and portable scanners. - Recommended scanning resolution: 300 dpi or higher. - Ensure correct fabric positioning during scanning. 3. **Bi-Consequence Processing:** Post-scan image processing to prepare textures for 3D use. --- ## Pattern Processing After Scanning This section focuses on processing scanned fabric patterns to ensure accuracy and continuity for 3D application. Key steps include: 1. **Color Correction:** Adjust color differences in Photoshop for realistic appearance. 2. **Pattern Repetition:** Convert scanned pattern into a correct quadrilateral for seamless repetition. - Proper quadrilateral patterns maintain continuity and realism. 3. **1:1 Ratio Maintenance:** Ensure DPI consistency between scanned and processed patterns to avoid size distortion. 4. **Plant Pattern Concept:** - A "plant" refers to hair-like texture elements over the base fabric. - Multiple images compose the plant: base fabric, hairline, and plant pattern. - Plant textures correspond to fabric physical properties. - Used for purchasing raw materials and matching lab texture rules. --- ## Plant Texture Attributes and Parameters This section explains texture attributes critical to fabric roughness and 3D effects, including hairline stickers, hallucination pictures, and highlight pictures. - **Hairline Sticker:** - Controls roughness perception. - Strength parameter range: -50 to +50. - 0 = no roughness. - Positive values increase roughness; negative values invert effect. - **Hallucination Picture:** - A grayscale image used to simulate 3D roughness on fabric. - Enhances depth perception in textures. - Parameters: - **Hallucination Degree:** Thickness of protrusions (0 to 2 mm). - **Movement:** Allows slight displacement to simulate texture floating, important for thick fabrics like wool. - **Cutting Height:** Threshold for geometric shape cuts on the sticker. - **Particle Structure:** Controls the horizontal grid size for 3D effect; affects image delicacy and memory consumption. - **Continuity:** Ensures seamless gaps after applying hallucination effects.

chunks.content: - **Hallucination Picture:** - A grayscale image used to simulate 3D roughness on fabric. - Enhances depth perception in textures. - Parameters: - **Hallucination Degree:** Thickness of protrusions (0 to 2 mm). - **Movement:** Allows slight displacement to simulate texture floating, important for thick fabrics like wool. - **Cutting Height:** Threshold for geometric shape cuts on the sticker. - **Particle Structure:** Controls the horizontal grid size for 3D effect; affects image delicacy and memory consumption. - **Continuity:** Ensures seamless gaps after applying hallucination effects. - **Highlight Picture:** - Defines surface brightness and reflection intensity. - Black areas = brightest; white areas = unlit. - Controls: - **Strength:** Reflection intensity. - **Roughness:** Surface roughness; higher values increase luminosity. - **Reflection Intensity:** Amount of light reflected; max around 70 for strong effect. --- ## Software Tools for Texture Processing: PixPlant and Photoshop This section introduces PixPlant and Photoshop workflows for fabric texture refinement and 3D sticker generation. - **PixPlant:** - Used for continuous fabric color processing and seamless pattern generation. - Supports seed file import (scanned pattern). - Parameters include resolution (300 dpi or 600 dpi), sample size, and pattern repetition options. - Generates simulation patterns and highlight maps for 3D stickers. - Allows brightness level selection for reflective effects. - **Photoshop:** - Used for color correction, four-way continuous editing, pattern repetition, and compounding materials. - Tools: - Transparent cutting tool for selecting quadrilateral points. - Filters > Other > Subtract for pattern smoothing. - Pixel adjustments via Alt key for gap filling. - Layer techniques for compounding hard flower fabrics or combining drawings with base materials. - Highlight creation and fade effect adjustments. - Adding 3D effects by layering white (high saturation) and black (low saturation) fills and adjusting saturation radius. --- ## Processing Different Fabric Types This section details methods for handling various fabric types and their specific texture challenges. ### Hollow and Plastic Fabrics - Use irregular pattern options in PixPlant for fabrics like hollow sand. - Remove irregular parts and generate seamless patterns carefully. - Adjust surface smoothness, highlight patterns, and hairline ranges for realistic effects. - Avoid low particle structure values to manage memory consumption. ### Hard Flower Fabrics - Process color and pattern separately. - Use Photoshop and PixPlant for generating continuous line drawings and 3D stickers. - Pay attention to contrasting colors for automatic line drawing generation. - Manual editing may be required for uniform colors. ### Compounded Materials - Use Photoshop layering for combining multiple texture elements. - Adjust transparency and reflection for materials like sand and dots. - Composite textures with base and overlay stickers for complex fabrics. --- ## Importing and Applying Textures in CLO This section explains how to integrate processed textures into CLO projects for final rendering. - Import scanned and processed images (texture, highlight, hairline) into CLO. - Drag texture images into fabric layers. - Adjust shadow effects by layering textures and setting intensity (e.g., 50 for visible shadows). - Use highlight images to control reflection and surface brightness.

chunks.content: - Composite textures with base and overlay stickers for complex fabrics. --- ## Importing and Applying Textures in CLO This section explains how to integrate processed textures into CLO projects for final rendering. - Import scanned and processed images (texture, highlight, hairline) into CLO. - Drag texture images into fabric layers. - Adjust shadow effects by layering textures and setting intensity (e.g., 50 for visible shadows). - Use highlight images to control reflection and surface brightness. - Adjust reflection intensity and roughness values for desired fabric appearance. - Render fabrics to view 3D effects such as bubble gauze or lace. - Save fabric files in CLO-specific formats (e.g., ZF, AB). --- ## Creating 3D Stickers and Embroidery Effects This section covers methods for generating 3D stickers and embroidery textures using hallucination pictures and blur filters. - Merge base pattern and blur-filtered image for softness. - Apply hallucination pictures with appropriate levels (1 to 1.5 mm) for 3D depth. - Use PNG images as egg-picking stickers on costumes. - Distinguish between plant textures and sticker effects (embroidery). - Quadruple continuity ensures seamless pattern repetition. --- ## Advanced Techniques and Additional Notes - **PVC Laser Fabric:** Create by adding PVC laser effects and setting property type to metal for enhanced reflection. - **Embroidery Patterns:** Require dedicated patterns; size adjusted via pattern editor. - **Invisible Zippers:** Sewn shut with zipper heads added as accessories. - **Diamond Pasting:** 3D effect available; requires specific processing. - **Fabric Measuring Instruments:** Test physical properties like stretch and drape; data used in fabric calculation models. - **Displacement Maps:** Must have black background for zero displacement; white or gray areas indicate displacement. - **Wrinkle Effects:** Not covered in this session; addressed in future lessons. --- ## Summary of Key Terms - **3D Sticker:** A texture map combining base pattern, hairline, hallucination, and highlight images to simulate realistic fabric surfaces. - **Hallucination Picture:** Grayscale map that adds 3D roughness perception. - **Plant Pattern:** Hair-like texture overlay enhancing depth and realism. - **PixPlant:** Software tool for seamless texture generation and 3D sticker creation. - **Four-Way Continuity:** Method for seamless pattern repetition by matching four corner points. - **Particle Structure:** Parameter controlling granularity of 3D hallucination effect grids. - **Reflection Intensity and Roughness:** Parameters controlling light reflection and surface texture appearance. --- This document provides comprehensive technical guidance for fabric texture processing in CLO, ensuring realistic and physically accurate 3D clothing visualization.

Key steps include: 1. **Color Correction:** Adjust color differences in Photoshop for realistic appearance. 2. **Pattern Repetition:** Convert scanned pattern into a correct quadrilateral for seamless repetition. - Proper quadrilateral patterns maintain continuity and realism. 3. **1:1 Ratio Maintenance:** Ensure DPI consistency between scanned and processed patterns to avoid size distortion. 4. **Plant Pattern Concept:** - A "plant" refers to hair-like texture elements over the base fabric. - Multiple images compose the plant: base fabric, hairline, and plant pattern. - Plant textures correspond to fabric physical properties. - Used for purchasing raw materials and matching lab texture rules. --- ## Plant Texture Attributes and Parameters This section explains texture attributes critical to fabric roughness and 3D effects, including hairline stickers, hallucination pictures, and highlight pictures. - **Hairline Sticker:** - Controls roughness perception. - Strength parameter range: -50 to +50. - 0 = no roughness. - Positive values increase roughness; negative values invert effect. - **Hallucination Picture:** - A grayscale image used to simulate 3D roughness on fabric. - Enhances depth perception in textures. - Parameters: - **Hallucination Degree:** Thickness of protrusions (0 to 2 mm). - **Movement:** Allows slight displacement to simulate texture floating, important for thick fabrics like wool. - **Cutting Height:** Threshold for geometric shape cuts on the sticker. - **Particle Structure:** Controls the horizontal grid size for 3D effect; affects image delicacy and memory consumption. - **Continuity:** Ensures seamless gaps after applying hallucination effects. - **Highlight Picture:** - Defines surface brightness and reflection intensity. - Black areas = brightest; white areas = unlit. - Controls: - **Strength:** Reflection intensity. - **Roughness:** Surface roughness; higher values increase luminosity. - **Reflection Intensity:** Amount of light reflected; max around 70 for strong effect. --- ## Software Tools for Texture Processing: PixPlant and Photoshop This section introduces PixPlant and Photoshop workflows for fabric texture refinement and 3D sticker generation. - **PixPlant:** - Used for continuous fabric color processing and seamless pattern generation. - Supports seed file import (scanned pattern). - Parameters include resolution (300 dpi or 600 dpi), sample size, and pattern repetition options. - Generates simulation patterns and highlight maps for 3D stickers. - Allows brightness level selection for reflective effects. - **Photoshop:** - Used for color correction, four-way continuous editing, pattern repetition, and compounding materials. - Tools: - Transparent cutting tool for selecting quadrilateral points. - Filters > Other > Subtract for pattern smoothing. - Pixel adjustments via Alt key for gap filling. - Layer techniques for compounding hard flower fabrics or combining drawings with base materials. - Highlight creation and fade effect adjustments. - Adding 3D effects by layering white (high saturation) and black (low saturation) fills and adjusting saturation radius. --- ## Processing Different Fabric Types This section details methods for handling various fabric types and their specific texture challenges. ### Hollow and Plastic Fabrics - Use irregular pattern options in PixPlant for fabrics like hollow sand. - Remove irregular parts and generate seamless patterns carefully. - Adjust surface smoothness, highlight patterns, and hairline ranges for realistic effects. - Avoid low particle structure values to manage memory consumption. ### Hard Flower Fabrics - Process color and pattern separately. - Use Photoshop and PixPlant for generating continuous line drawings and 3D stickers. - Pay attention to contrasting colors for automatic line drawing generation. - Manual editing may be required for uniform colors. ### Compounded Materials - Use Photoshop layering for combining multiple texture elements. - Adjust transparency and reflection for materials like sand and dots. - Composite textures with base and overlay stickers for complex fabrics. --- ## Importing and Applying Textures in CLO This section explains how to integrate processed textures into CLO projects for final rendering. - Import scanned and processed images (texture, highlight, hairline) into CLO. - Drag texture images into fabric layers. - Adjust shadow effects by layering textures and setting intensity (e.g., 50 for visible shadows). - Use highlight images to control reflection and surface brightness. - Adjust reflection intensity and roughness values for desired fabric appearance. - Render fabrics to view 3D effects such as bubble gauze or lace. - Save fabric files in CLO-specific formats (e.g., ZF, AB). --- ## Creating 3D Stickers and Embroidery Effects This section covers methods for generating 3D stickers and embroidery textures using hallucination pictures and blur filters. - Merge base pattern and blur-filtered image for softness. - Apply hallucination pictures with appropriate levels (1 to 1.5 mm) for 3D depth. - Use PNG images as egg-picking stickers on costumes. - Distinguish between plant textures and sticker effects (embroidery). - Quadruple continuity ensures seamless pattern repetition. --- ## Advanced Techniques and Additional Notes - **PVC Laser Fabric:** Create by adding PVC laser effects and setting property type to metal for enhanced reflection. - **Embroidery Patterns:** Require dedicated patterns; size adjusted via pattern editor. - **Invisible Zippers:** Sewn shut with zipper heads added as accessories. - **Diamond Pasting:** 3D effect available; requires specific processing. - **Fabric Measuring Instruments:** Test physical properties like stretch and drape; data used in fabric calculation models. - **Displacement Maps:** Must have black background for zero displacement; white or gray areas indicate displacement. - **Wrinkle Effects:** Not covered in this session; addressed in future lessons. --- ## Summary of Key Terms - **3D Sticker:** A texture map combining base pattern, hairline, hallucination, and highlight images to simulate realistic fabric surfaces. - **Hallucination Picture:** Grayscale map that adds 3D roughness perception. - **Plant Pattern:** Hair-like texture overlay enhancing depth and realism. - **PixPlant:** Software tool for seamless texture generation and 3D sticker creation. - **Four-Way Continuity:** Method for seamless pattern repetition by matching four corner points. - **Particle Structure:** Parameter controlling granularity of 3D hallucination effect grids. - **Reflection Intensity and Roughness:** Parameters controlling light reflection and surface texture appearance. --- This document provides comprehensive technical guidance for fabric texture processing in CLO, ensuring realistic and physically accurate 3D clothing visualization.
